title: Indian Women Boxers Chase First Asian Games Gold Since Mary Kom's 2014 Win
excerpt: An 11-member squad led by Lovlina Borgohain heads to Nagoya with momentum from Glasgow and a dominant Asian Championships — and a 12-year gold drought to end.
body:
• India has named an 11-member boxing squad for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, led by Olympic bronze medallist Lovlina Borgohain, with five women and six men across the weight classes.
  • The women's team is chasing India's first Asian Games boxing gold since Mary Kom's 2014 triumph, after topping the Asian Championships in Mongolia earlier this year with 10 medals.
  • The squad trained at a pre-Games camp in Nishio City, Japan, from September 8 to 16, and was picked through a new sparring-based assessment system with five-judge scoring.
  • The Commonwealth Games in Glasgow this summer gave the group momentum; Nagoya's stronger continental field, led by China, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, will be the real test.

A Twelve-Year Wait

No Indian woman has won Asian Games boxing gold since Mary Kom stood atop the podium in Incheon in 2014. In Nagoya, a new generation gets its chance to end that drought.

The Boxing Federation of India has named an 11-member squad for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which run from September 19 to October 4. The women's contingent — Sakshi Chaudhary (51kg), Preeti Pawar (54kg), Priya Ghanghas (60kg), Parveen Hooda (65kg) and Olympic bronze medallist Lovlina Borgohain (75kg) — carries the weight of that 12-year wait. The men's team comprises Jadumani Singh (55kg), Sachin Siwach (60kg), Sumit Kundu (70kg), Ankush Panghal (80kg), Kapil Pokhariya (90kg) and Narender Berwal (+90kg).

The squad was shaped through a revised selection process the federation introduced for the 2026 cycle: a sparring-based assessment scored by five judges, designed, the BFI said, to make evaluation more transparent. The boxers then completed a pre-Games training camp in Nishio City, Japan, from September 8 to 16, training alongside reserves and support staff.

Form Is on Their Side

There is genuine reason for optimism. Earlier this year, India's women topped the Asian Boxing Championships in Mongolia, finishing first in the medal standings with 10 medals — four gold, two silver and four bronze — with every boxer on the team returning with a medal. Meenakshi (48kg), Preeti (54kg), Priya (60kg) and Arundhati Choudhary (70kg) all won gold, under the guidance of coach Santiago Nieva.

Preeti's run in Mongolia was particularly striking: she outpointed three-time world champion Huang Hsiao-wen of Chinese Taipei 5-0, beating a Tokyo Olympic bronze medallist with complete control. Priya defeated North Korea's Won Un-gyong 3-0, and Arundhati beat Kazakhstan's Bakyt Seidish 4-1.

Parveen Hooda, who won Asian Championships gold and World Championships bronze before injury interrupted her career, arrives in Nagoya on a comeback arc after winning the World Boxing Cup Finals, where she beat Poland's world silver medallist Aneta Rygielska and Japan's Olympian Ayaka Taguchi.

"World Cup Finals was my comeback event as I had participated in an international level tournament after a long time due to injury. My opponents were very accomplished boxers, so the event was very good for me."

— Parveen Hooda, Indian boxer

The Glasgow Springboard

The Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, held from July 23 to August 2, gave this group confidence and momentum. But as analysts of the squad note, the Asian Games demand something different: adaptability, tactical discipline and the ability to handle opponents with established pedigree across the continent. China, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan remain the standard-setters in Asian boxing, and Glasgow's medals will count for little against them.

For Lovlina Borgohain, the Tokyo Olympic bronze medallist leading the squad, Nagoya is another chapter in a career that has carried Indian women's boxing since Mary Kom's era. The question for Indian boxing in Aichi-Nagoya is whether Glasgow's breakthrough can travel across a stronger continental field.

What to Watch

The first bell in Japan marks the beginning of that test. The women's middle and light-middle weights look India's strongest cards, and the new selection system's transparency will itself be judged by results. Twelve years after Mary Kom's gold, Indian boxing has depth, momentum and a settled squad — now it needs the one thing that has been missing: an Asian Games champion.
